descriptors.R: the sitting President, nominee of the party in power since 1861, which defends the Reconstruction amendments and federal enforcement against violent organizations in the South
descriptors.D: nominee of a reform breakaway from the governing party, also endorsed by the opposition party; a longtime newspaper editor calling for universal amnesty, civil service reform and local self-government in the South

compile_desc.D: the reform breakaway from the governing party, endorsed by the opposition party

others_line: Other candidates on some ballots, including a nominee of opposition-party holdouts who refused the endorsement (answer "other").
never_name: Grant, Henry Wilson, Greeley, Gratz Brown, Sumner, Schurz, O'Conor, Woodhull or Hendricks

slice_sources.men: 1870 census (Ninth Census) aged to November 1872, men 21+ outside the former Confederate states; the Fifteenth Amendment now let Black men vote everywhere; calibrated to certified returns.
slice_sources.women: No women could vote for president in 1872 (some who tried, in Rochester and elsewhere, were arrested); women 21+ shown for population only.
slice_sources.south-white: 1870 census aged to 1872, white adults in the former Confederate states, all now readmitted and voting by popular vote; most former Confederates had their disabilities lifted by the May 1872 amnesty; calibrated to certified returns.
slice_sources.black-south: 1870 census aged to 1872, Black adults in the former Confederate states; Black men voted under the Fifteenth Amendment and the federal Enforcement Acts, which had broken up much of the Klan by 1872.
slice_sources.immigrants: 1870 census aged to 1872, foreign-born white men not yet naturalized; many Midwestern, Western and Southern states let declarant aliens vote, elsewhere only naturalized men could.
